chunks: "A square wave is noisy because the sharp edges are really a huge stack of high-frequency sinusoids.
Ideal harmonics fall as one over n, so even a 10 megahertz clock has meaningful content out into the hundreds of MHz. On a real board those frequencies hit all the parasitics.
The edge charges trace capacitance, which pulls a current spike, I equals C dV/dt.
That spike flows through the inductance of the package and the return path, giving L di/dt disturbances on the supply and ground.
The same fast edges couple into neighbouring traces through mutual capacitance and inductance, and the current loop acts as a small antenna whose radiation grows with frequency squared.
To reduce noise, the biggest lever is slowing the edge, because high harmonics scale inversely with rise time.

I'd use a series resistor or slew-rate control, lower the frequency if the design allows, keep the current loop small with a solid return plane, add decoupling, filter or ferrite the lines that leave the board, and use differential signalling for fast links.
For a particular frequency, I can place a null on it: choosing a duty cycle of one over n kills the nth harmonic, and a rise time of one over f puts a null at f.
Otherwise I'd use a notch or LC trap, pick a ferrite whose impedance peaks there, or damp the resonance that's amplifying it."
